node.label: Anna Davin
node.date_label: Feminist History (1976) · Imperialism and Motherhood (1978) · Growing Up Poor (1996)
node.description: In “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978), Anna Davin argued that efforts to improve infant welfare in Britain were shaped by imperial competition and eugenic ideas about the population. She examined how maternal instruction put working-class mothers’ conduct under scrutiny while exposing tensions between their lives and reformers’ expectations. Muggeridge and Davidson describe the essay as pathbreaking and identify its influence on feminist histories of maternity care. Growing Up Poor: Home, School and Street in London, 1870–1914 (1996) reconstructs poor children’s everyday lives, especially girls’ work, schooling and family responsibilities, using institutional records, autobiography and oral testimony. Reviewer Dietrich Oberwittler praised its detailed history from below while noting that fathers, Sunday schools and cinema receive little or no attention. As Kelly Boyd recounts, Davin and Sally Alexander made feminist analysis central to History Workshop Journal in “Feminist History” (1976). In “Labouring Women: a reply to Eric Hobsbawm” (1979), Davin, Alexander and Eve Hostettler challenged Hobsbawm’s exclusion of wage-earning wives and women’s class agency, as Sonya O. Rose explains.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Feminist History” (1976), with Sally Alexander; “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978; reprinted 1997); “Labouring Women: a reply to Eric Hobsbawm” (1979), with Alexander and Eve Hostettler; “When is a Child Not a Child” (1990); Growing Up Poor: Home, School and Street in London, 1870–1914 (1996); “What is a child?” (1999).

proposed_edges.relationship: Davin recalls that Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963), especially its primary sources, inspired her decision to study history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, answers beginning “Always watching!” and “We went to Warwick” (HTML paragraphs at lines 249–250): “inspiring”. Retrospective testimony; no claim to a particular argument in Davin’s later books.
proposed_edges.map_label: The Making inspired her history studies

proposed_edges.relationship: Hobsbawm supervised Davin’s research leading to her childhood thesis (1992); she later recalled disagreement over his demand for more statistics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, paragraph beginning “Being a graduate student” and following answers (lines 280–288): “you need more statistics”. Archive biography dates submission to 1992. Thesis and supervision records unread; this is Davin’s recollection.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Labouring Women” (1979), Davin, Sally Alexander and Eve Hostettler challenged Hobsbawm’s exclusion of wage-earning wives and women’s class agency, as Sonya O. Rose explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Rose (1993), printed p. 156, paragraph beginning “This analysis” and notes 53–54: “excluded wage-earning wives” and “participation in class struggle”; note 54 points to reply p. 175. All three coauthors credited. Publisher byline read; original reply body unread. Do not infer that Hobsbawm accepted their criticism.

proposed_edges.relationship: Davin and Gareth Stedman Jones were founding coeditors of History Workshop Journal (1976).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bishopsgate RS 9 finding aid, PDF p. 2, Administrative/Biographical History, lists both among “The first editors”; Taylor (2025), paragraph beginning “History Workshop Journal was started in 1976”, independently confirms. Collective editorship, not a coauthored article or agreement on every position.

proposed_edges.relationship: As a founding editor of History Workshop Journal (1976), Davin pursued collective, accessible historical writing, as she recalls in “Making Histories” (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2025 interview, answers to “Was that part of what you were trying to do” and “So the collective” (lines 324–328); “not about the individual but about the collective”. Founding date independently supported by Taylor and archive. Existing History Workshop roster row preserved; no duplicate Anna Davin edge exists.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Sally Alexander, Davin made feminist analysis central to the journal’s programme in “Feminist History” (1976), as Kelly Boyd recounts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Boyd, “Background and founding”, paragraph beginning “Scholars themselves often worked together”, sentence beginning “The first volume” and note 9: “central a feminist analysis”. A named historical reader supports this limited programme claim; original editorial body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978) connected infant welfare and maternal roles to imperial and eugenic politics, an intervention Muggeridge and Davidson identify as pathbreaking.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Muggeridge and Davidson (2026), section I, paragraphs beginning “Anna Davin’s pathbreaking article” and “Davin identified”, notes 6–8: “imperialist and eugenicist discourses”. Substantive reception of the 1978 essay; original and 1997 reprint unread in this assignment. No general derivation of gender history asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Labouring Women” (1979), coauthored with Sally Alexander and Eve Hostettler, challenged labour history’s exclusion of married women as workers and participants in class struggle, as Rose explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Rose (1993), pp. 155–156, especially p. 156 paragraph beginning “This analysis” and note 54. Field-level methodological intervention distinguished from the personal Hobsbawm critique. The 1979 article is known through this named reader and checked byline; full original unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Married women as workers and class actors

proposed_edges.relationship: Growing Up Poor (1996) used autobiographies and interviews from oral-history archives to reconstruct children’s everyday lives, as Dietrich Oberwittler’s review documents.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Oberwittler (1999), p. 761 final paragraph: “Autobiographien und Interviews” and “Oral History-Archive”; p. 762 opening discusses what interview material adds to accounts of poverty. Read complete review in publisher OCR. Book unread; no claim that Davin conducted every interview she used.
proposed_edges.map_label: Oral testimony and poor children’s lives

proposed_edges.relationship: In his London Review of Books review of Growing Up Poor (1996), Porter praised Davin’s reconstruction of the makeshift family economies and changing role of poor London children, but wished she had been more speculative and had said more about fathers and about charities, churches, clubs and cheap commercial culture.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the journal’s own site: Roy Porter, “I ain’t a child”, London Review of Books 18, no. 17 (5 September 1996), a single-book review of Growing Up Poor: Home, School and Street 1870–1914 (Rivers Oram, 1996). Paragraph 1 (beginning “Anna Davin has risen admirably to the challenges facing the historian of working-class life in London”) praises her handling of Booth, school records, autobiography and her own oral-history tapes. Paragraph 6 (“She has done so with a strong historical sympathy”) says she “carefully reconstructs old makeshift ways” and aims “to trace the changing role of children in the family economy”; paragraph 7 states “Davin’s point” that the new domestic order “took hold only slowly and after protracted conflict”. Paragraph 17 of 18 carries the criticism: “Davin sticks close to her sources, and sometimes one hankers after a more speculative style”, adding that more might have been said about the role of fathers and about “charities and churches, clubs and cheap commercial culture”, and regretting that Steedman’s Strange Dislocations (1995) appeared too late for her to use; the paragraph closes in praise (“intimate, intense and often poignant”). A mixed review that engages the book’s argument, so critique rather than comparison. Porter’s comparisons with Anna Clark, Carolyn Steedman and Stedman Jones are his own framing and are not proposed as Davin relationships. Davin’s book was not reread for this edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anna Davin’s ‘Imperialism and Motherhood’ (1978) helped establish historical study of maternity care by examining infant welfare, imperial and eugenic concerns, and class tensions between mothers and reformers, as assessed by Anna Muggeridge and Ruth Davidson (2026).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open body text and relevant notes. The authors identify Davin’s analysis of early maternity provision and its subsequent uptake. This supports a contribution to medical and health history specifically through maternity and infant welfare. It does not establish influence on every later author mentioned. The pre-existing women’s and gender-history pairs are excluded.
